title: Standard Form: Read the Structure, Not Just the Symbols

scenes.title: What does 3x + 2y = 12 actually tell us?
body: Two variable contributions combine to one fixed total.
scenes.narration: Suppose you see three x plus two y equals twelve. What is standard form actually telling you? Here’s the idea: standard form organizes a linear relationship so the two variable contributions sit together on one side, and their fixed total sits on the other. The pattern is A x plus B y equals C.

scenes.title: The sign belongs to the coefficient
scenes.narration: This is where students often mix things up. In six x minus five y equals eighteen, B is negative five, not positive five. The sign is part of the coefficient because the term is really negative five times y. C is eighteen because it is the standalone constant on the other side.

scenes.title: Why the form works
body: Each ordered pair on the line makes the same total 12.
scenes.narration: Notice why this form represents a line. Every solution pair x comma y balances the same equation. For example, two comma three gives three times two plus two times three, which is six plus six equals twelve. Standard form is not just a layout; it describes all points whose weighted contributions add to the same constant.

scenes.title: A missing variable can have coefficient zero
body: A and B cannot both be zero.
scenes.substitution: 0y disappears, but the structure is still linear
scenes.narration: Another common confusion is thinking both variables must visibly appear. If you have three x equals fifteen, you can write it as three x plus zero y equals fifteen. So B can be zero. The rule is only that A and B cannot both be zero, because then there would be no variable relationship left.

scenes.title: Read, check, and interpret
body: Check a solution by substituting both coordinates.
Keep each sign attached to its term.
scenes.equation: Ax + By = C = variable contributions → fixed total
scenes.narration: So when you read standard form, identify the x coefficient with its sign, the y coefficient with its sign, and then the constant. If a problem gives a point, substitute both coordinates to check whether the balance is true. The big idea is that standard form packages two variable contributions into one fixed total.
